title: ‘Goodbye Julia’ Director on Reaching for ‘Wider Audiences’ in Sudanese Period Drama ‘About Love & September Laws’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Sudanese filmmaker Mohamed Kordofani, whose debut feature “Goodbye Julia” premiered in Cannes’ Un Certain Regard sidebar, has attracted a raft of p
body:
Sudanese filmmaker Mohamed Kordofani, whose debut feature “Goodbye Julia” premiered in Cannes’ Un Certain Regard sidebar, has attracted a raft of partners for his follow-up “About Love & September Laws,” which he’ll be taking to Rome’s MIA Market, running from Oct. 19-23.

	Produced by Klozium Studios, the production outfit he launched in 2020 with “Goodbye Julia” co-producer Khalid Awad, the film will reunite the core creative team behind Kordofani’s acclaimed debut, including co-producers Marc Irmer, of France’s Dolce Vita; Michael Henrichs, of German production company DGS; and Issraa Elkogali, of Sweden’s RiverFlower. Also on board are “Goodbye Julia” cinematographer Pierre De Villiers, editor Heba Osman, sound designer Rana Eid and co-writer Khaled Alwaleed.
	

	“About Love & September Laws” is the second installment in a planned trilogy that tells the modern history of Sudan. Set in 1983, it follows an African American journalist, Carter, who arrives in Khartoum on a mission to revive a struggling newspaper. There he reunites with Nouri, an old friend he hasn’t seen in 10 years, now an idealistic doctor who serves as an ideological counterpoint to the jaded reporter.


	Things grow complicated when Carter falls for Fatin, his newly hired translator, unaware that she is Nouri’s ex-wife. The fragile romance collides with the sudden weight of politics when Sharia law is imposed across Sudan, and Nouri finds himself facing the death sentence when he refuses a court order to amputate a thief’s hand.

	When Carter uncovers a story that could expose the regime’s hypocrisy and save Nouri’s life, he’s forced to choose between the career he came to rebuild, the friendship that gave him a home in Sudan and a love he is only beginning to realize he can’t afford to lose.
	

	Speaking to Variety ahead of MIA, Kordofani explains that while “About Love & September Laws” is set against the backdrop of a pivotal moment in Sudanese history, at its core “it’s a story about three people who are entangled in different kinds of love.”

	The director’s groundbreaking debut was the first Sudanese feature to make the official selection at the Cannes Film Festival. Executive produced by Academy Award winner Lupita N’yongo, the film won the Un Certain Regard section’s Freedom Prize along with 65 other international plaudits, including audience awards at El Gouna and Singapore. In a rave review, Variety’s Jessica Kiang praised the “engrossing” drama as a “well-performed deep cut into Sudan’s recent history [that] unfolds like a morality thriller.”

	As with “Goodbye Julia,” which takes place in Khartoum during the six years prior to the 2011 secession of South Sudan, Kordofani’s latest again looks to “bridge the personal and the political, the local and the global, the past and the present,” he says. However, after his first feature struggled to break into the U.S. and U.K. markets, the director says he’s determined to “reach even wider audiences.”

	“Even before ‘Goodbye Julia,’ I’ve always wanted to make films that are for the mainstream but still hold artistic value, educational value — [sharing] something about my country that people don’t know,” he says. “I still want to do the things I want to do, but I want to make the film more accessible. The wider the reach, the better.”



	

					“Goodbye Julia” won the Freedom Prize in Cannes’ Un Certain Regard
	



	Last December, “About Love & September Laws” scooped a trio of prizes at the Red Sea Film Festival’s industry Souk Awards. In Rome, where it’s among the 12 projects taking part in MIA’s Film Co-Production Market, Kordofani said he’s particularly “looking for partners that can [build a] bridge to the United States.”

	“It’s a film with an American lead. It’s predominantly English. I think, in the development stage, I should start building these bridges, not only for casting but also for the journey of the film and presenting the film [to a U.S. audience],” he says.

	Central to that will be the lead role of Carter, a former Black Panther and disillusioned reporter who’s “lost faith in bigger causes and bigger movements,” says Kordofani. Opposite him is Nouri, the idealistic doctor, whose refusal to enforce a Sharia court order puts his life in jeopardy. “There’s this clash of personalities,” says the director, characterizing the film as a “moral drama” where “slowly, the politics will seep into their story and guide how the story unfolds.”
	

	A winner of Variety’s MENA Talent of the Year Award in 2023, Kordofani is among the many Sudanese who were forced to flee the country amid the ongoing war. Now based in Nairobi, where he and Awad have established their production shingle Klozium Studios, he nevertheless feels an obligation to his homeland, saying, “I do feel a responsibility to talk about Sudan.”

	“Living apart from my family, I continue to…search for purpose through filmmaking,” he says. “And especially now, as war rages on, I feel an urgent responsibility to preserve and create our own narrative — before it is stolen, silenced or rewritten by others.”

	“About Love & September Laws,” he adds, offers “a platform to engage directly with the Western world, not as an outsider telling Sudan’s story, but as someone inviting them into a shared conversation about freedom, sacrifice, love and truth-seeking.”

schema.headline: ‘Goodbye Julia’ Director on Reaching for ‘Wider Audiences’ in Sudanese Period Drama ‘About Love & September Laws’ (EXCLUSIVE)

title: ‘Lilly,’ Starring Patricia Clarkson, to Open London’s Women and the World Intl. Film Festival
description: Rachel Feldman’s “Lilly,” starring Patricia Clarkson, will open the third edition of the Women and the World International Film Festival, which run
body:
Rachel Feldman’s “Lilly,” starring Patricia Clarkson, will open the third edition of the Women and the World International Film Festival, which runs in London from Nov. 5-12.

	Highlights of the program, which puts women’s authorship at its center, include the world premiere of Sigrid Andrea P. Bernardo’s “Laya,” alongside premieres of Marina Kunarova’s “The Nomad’s Legacy” and Flaminia Graziadei’s “A Year in London.”


	In a statement, Ksenia Bugrimova, the festival director, said, “The age of the ‘good girl’ is over. Cinema needs women who are complicated, instinctive, ambitious, vulnerable, fearless and free – women who do not ask permission to take up space.
	

	“We believe there should simply be more films by women in the world – and more opportunities for those films to reach audiences. Celebrating women is important, but celebration alone is not enough. We want to support them, advocate for them and connect their work directly with audiences and the international film industry.”

	The jury includes David Gyasi, British actor and producer; Olwen Fouéré, Irish actor, writer and director; MyAnna Buring, British-Swedish actor; Elena Andreicheva, documentary filmmaker and producer; Denise Parkinson, VP, sales and marketing global, Variety; David Martinez, film publicity executive; Rebecca del Tufo, co-founder and co-director, ScreenCraft Works; and Victoria Emslie, British actor and producer.

	In addition to the screening program, WWIFF said it is expanding its efforts to provide a platform for emerging filmmakers and creative talent through collaborations with University College London, LAMDA, Film London and BFI Network.
	

	The festival’s 2025 edition attracted 2,450 attendees and closed with the U.K. premiere of Scarlett Johansson’s directorial debut “Eleanor the Great.”

schema.headline: ‘Lilly,’ Starring Patricia Clarkson, to Open London’s Women and the World Intl. Film Festival

title: Human-AI Indian Music Label Raagverse Launches With ‘Janaa Hai Toh Jao’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Raagverse, a new Indian music label that pairs human songwriting with AI production tools, will release its first album, “Janaa Hai Toh Jao,” on Oc
body:
Raagverse, a new Indian music label that pairs human songwriting with AI production tools, will release its first album, “Janaa Hai Toh Jao,” on Oct. 20.

	The label is the latest venture from Amita Madhvani, CEO of Equinox Virtual, which she co-founded with Ram Madhvani. Equinox Virtual is the arm of Equinox Films and Ram Madhvani Films that develops projects using artificial intelligence and immersive technology.


	The debut album has three songs: the title track, “Koi Keh De Usse” and “Tere Liye.” Mamta Javkar wrote the lyrics for all of them. “Janaa Hai Toh Jao” leads the release, which will be available on YouTube Music, Apple Music, Spotify and other major streaming services.
	

	Raagverse is built on a creative process that keeps people in charge by design. Each song starts with Javkar’s words and the feeling or idea behind them. AI then comes in as one of several tools used to shape that material into a finished recording. People make the calls on lyrics, creative direction and the mood each track should carry.

	Madhvani said her first experiments with AI as part of a wider creative process came on “Mohini – Khud Se Pyaar,” a musical microdrama Equinox Virtual made with the technology. “What stayed with me from that experience was that technology could give us new ways to execute an idea, but the idea itself still needed to come from somewhere deeply human. With Raagverse, I wanted to take that thought into music,” she said. “For me, that is where this gets exciting. It is not human creativity versus AI. It is about seeing what becomes possible when human imagination leads and technology helps us take it somewhere new.”
	

	Raagverse is registered as an intellectual property. Equinox Virtual plans to keep using it as a home for original music made the same way, with software expanding what the team can do while the songwriting stays in human hands.

	The label joins a slate at Equinox Virtual that also includes a virtual reality experience built with AI and drawing on Indian text “Bhagavad Gita.” The company’s aim is to use new technology to create fresh story formats and original Indian content for a global audience.

schema.headline: Human-AI Indian Music Label Raagverse Launches With ‘Janaa Hai Toh Jao’ (EXCLUSIVE)

title: ‘Oz’ Creator Tom Fontana to Showrun Vatican Drama Series Based on ‘The Devil’s Business’ Book as Fabel Entertainment Scores Rights (EXCLUSIVE)
description: “Oz” creator Tom Fontana is set to create and showrun a new Vatican drama series based on Emanuele Midolo’s forthcoming novel “The Devil’s Business
body:
“Oz” creator Tom Fontana is set to create and showrun a new Vatican drama series based on Emanuele Midolo’s forthcoming novel “The Devil’s Business” after Fabel Entertainment scored book rights. 

	“The Devil’s Business” — which is set to publish via Century in June 2028 — centers on Archbishop Paul Marcinkus, the American clergyman known as “The Pope’s Bodyguard.” Midolo is an award-winning investigations correspondent with The Sunday Times’ Insight team, whose reporting has led to political resignations in the U.K. and nominations for the U.K. Society of Editors’ Scoop of the Year and Investigation of the Year.
	

	Set in the 1980s, the series will follow Marckinkus from his beginnings as Pope Paul VI’s unofficial bodyguard to his tenure at the helm of the Vatican’s finances. As is told in Midolo’s book, Marcinkus — who was known to say, “You can’t run the Church on Hail Marys” — “wielded immense power during an era of astonishing scandals involving embezzlement, money laundering, kidnapping, poison and alleged staged suicide,” according to a press release.


	Fabel Entertainment is leading development and will produce alongside the Italy-based Picomedia, a Fremantle company. 

	“I’ve wanted to tell this story for decades,” said Fontana, who is also known for his work on “Homicide: Life on the Street” and “Borgia.” “I love this world, and Emanuele’s book has given us a new window into Marcinkus. I’m grateful for the chance to finally bring to life a complex man who lives in the grey area between sinner and saint. His is a cautionary tale for our swiftly changing times.”
	

	Added Henrik Bastin, CEO of Fabel Entertainment: “Ten pages into Manu’s book proposal, we knew we wanted to make this series. In a way it’s a very American story — rising from the top from humble beginnings — only this time, the setting is the Vatican and the man is doing the Pope’s dirty work. Tom Fontana was our first and last call. No showrunner knows the politics of Rome and the Vatican better, and we’re thrilled to have his unparalleled wit and fearlessness bringing it to life.”

	For Midolo, working with Fontana is a dream come true “as a longstanding ‘Oz’ fan since I was about 10,” he said. “The archbishop at the heart of this true story, Paul Marcinkus, was a larger-than-life figure who makes the fictional cardinals of ‘Conclave’ look like innocent schoolboys. I can’t wait to see him in action.”

	Roberto Sessa, Founder & CEO, Picomedia, said: “Marcinkus was an American, but his story takes us deep into a chapter of Italian history that still raises difficult questions. It’s a story with international reach and very Italian roots. We’re delighted to be working with Fabel and Tom to bring both to the screen.”

	Midolo is represented by Eugenie Furniss at 42. Raffaella De Angelis, head of literary acquisitions, global drama at Fremantle spearheaded the literary acquisition for Fabel Entertainment. Fontana is represented by UTA and Fabel Entertainment is represented by CAA.

title: ‘Percy Jackson’ Stars Will Attend Lucca Comics, Seeking to ‘Get Up Close and Personal With Their Fans,’ Geek Meet’s Film and TV Chief Says
description: When “Percy Jackson” series stars Walker Scobell, Leah Sava Jeffries and Aryan Simhadri make the trek to Italy’s Lucca Comics and Games Festival in
body:
When “Percy Jackson” series stars Walker Scobell, Leah Sava Jeffries and Aryan Simhadri make the trek to Italy’s Lucca Comics and Games Festival in late October – to unveil unseen footage ahead of the Nov. 20 release of Season 3 of “Percy Jackson and the Olympians” – they will travel to a unique geek meet held within the 16th century walls of a medieval Tuscan town that is attended by more than 200,000 fans each year.

	This massive event dedicated to fandom, cosplay and the whole world of comics, including movies and TV, is the biggest pop culture festival in Europe. Lucca in recent years has reached a level of relevance for Hollywood and the Asian industry that is second to none.
	

	Variety speaks to Giovanni Cova, who is head of Milan-based entertainment marketing company QMI that leads programming of Lucca’s film and TV strand, about how the event is bolstering its status as an unmissable launching pad at a time when the role of traditional festivals as promotional vehicles is being questioned.

	
		Why are Hollywood studios and streamers choosing Lucca for their big launches?	

	This year we are, of course, absolutely delighted to have Disney’s support and to serve as a key stop on a major promotional tour, in this case, for “Percy Jackson.” I believe that, in the grand scheme of things, this further confirms that Lucca has become an essential international stage to unveil major series released in the autumn season. In recent years, we have served as “a” — if not “the” — primary showcase for titles like “Stranger Things,” “Squid Game,” “Wednesday” and “The Lord of the Rings.” Lucca has firmly established itself as a constant presence on the global promotional circuit for studios and streaming platforms, which is something that gives us great satisfaction. The fact that such significant promotional events are taking place here in Europe, in Italy, and specifically in a city like Lucca is truly gratifying. Of course, we must thank the local offices of the major studios and streaming services. They have effectively communicated the importance of Lucca to the decision-makers back in Los Angeles.
	
	
		What makes Lucca stand out? What gives it such global reach?	

	Given the high profile of the guests who attend Lucca, the media exposure we generate is truly significant. Furthermore, the unique nature of the Lucca festival, the photo opportunities it provides, and the chance for talent to get up close and personal with their actual fans is, in my view, absolutely priceless. You can see this in the images from the launches of series or films in Lucca. They travel around the world because they are so distinctive. Very different from the typical red-carpet scene. Seeing the ancient Piazza San Michele packed with people, and witnessing those genuine encounters between the cast and the audience. That is the unique experience we offer to the entertainment world.
	
		Talk to me about Lucca’s other “big gets” this year	

	Well, it’s fantastic for us to have Frank Miller here. He loves Italy; he loves Lucca, and he’s returning for what I believe is the fourth or fifth time. We couldn’t be happier. Frank truly embodies the values of Lucca and the types of genre we love. We also have talents like Kore-eda [Hirokazu] who this year attended the Cannes Film Festival for one type of project [“Sheep in the Box”], but is then coming to Lucca for another [“Look Back”]. Then there’s Joe Manganiello, who, much like Frank, is a huge fan of Lucca. He embodies the festival’s spirit, spanning cinema, video games and tabletop games. He really represents the multimedia nature of Lucca.
	
		Lucca transcends these boundaries. Talk to me about the different types of experiences it offers.	

	Another crucial aspect of Lucca is that, beyond the screenings and the presence of talent, the festival offers the public a chance to truly engage with a property. To experience it firsthand. There are pavilions and live installations where the audience can immerse themselves in these worlds. We’ll have a “Harry Potter” experience, a K-pop-themed experience from Netflix, and a pavilion from Crunchyroll, which, in addition to hosting numerous premieres, allows fans to engage directly with its content. We’ll also see this with “Percy Jackson,” from Disney, as well as with “Dexter” for Paramount+. Ultimately, these installations, these immersive, interactive and event-driven experiences are just as significant as the presence of talent.
	
	
		At a time when the promotional value of festivals is coming into question what’s keeping Lucca so relevant?	

	In my view, the main difference between Lucca and traditional festivals is that, at Lucca, there is no filter between the content, the talent and the audience. Traditional festivals are events where content is typically presented to industry professionals and the press, who then act as intermediaries, bringing that content to the general public. In Lucca, instead, film criticism is not part of the festival’s DNA. For Lucca, presenting content simply means bringing it directly to the fans. There is no mediation by industry insiders, critics or film journalists. And I say this without being judgmental. It is simply that we are not that type of festival. Consequently, we don’t have to worry about generating “bad press,” as that falls outside our scope and purpose. We simply provide studios with the opportunity to connect directly with the audience, whether through content or specific activations.

schema.headline: ‘Percy Jackson’ Stars Will Attend Lucca Comics, Seeking to ‘Get Up Close and Personal With Their Fans,’ Geek Meet’s Film and TV Chief Says

title: ‘Line of Duty’ Director Douglas Mackinnon Preps Edinburgh-Set Paramedic Drama ‘BurnTime,’ Builds Slate at Rugged Island Films (EXCLUSIVE)
description: “Line of Duty” and “Good Omens” director Douglas Mackinnon is prepping an Edinburgh-set paramedic drama that’s part of a growing slate at his recent
body:
“Line of Duty” and “Good Omens” director Douglas Mackinnon is prepping an Edinburgh-set paramedic drama that’s part of a growing slate at his recently launched production outfit Rugged Island Films. Mackinnon will be presenting the series in the Drama Co-Production Forum at Rome’s MIA Market, which runs Oct. 19 – 23.“BurnTime” is a 6 x 60’ limited series set over six consecutive night shifts during the Edinburgh Festival, a raucous, month-long celebration of the arts in the Scottish capital. The series centers on 35-year-old Kylie MacDonald, a newly trained paramedic working her first shift in the so-called blue light cavalry, racing to save lives in her ambulance — even as a mystery surrounding a tragic episode from her past threatens to upend the life she’s carefully built.Speaking to Variety ahead of the market, Mackinnon says the show takes its title from the chronic burnout that afflicts emergency workers on the job. “The amount of time that paramedics last in the U.K. on average is 18 months…because it’s so stressful and so chaotic and so messy for their lives,” he says.“BurnTime” combines a strain of dark comedy with the propulsive energy that was a hallmark of Mackinnon’s two-year stint at the BBC’s “Line of Duty,” with the TV veteran saying, “Pain and laughter is the world that we’re in.”Central to the storyline is the Edinburgh Festival, and “the weird and the wonderful people” it brings to the Scottish capital every year, according to Mackinnon. “The festival is like a character, not just a backdrop,” he says, channeling George Clooney to compare the show’s madcap narrative possibilities to those of another well-known hospital drama.“‘The great thing about “E.R.” is that you could be walking down a corridor, open a door and there’s a Polish choir singing [in the room]. Then you just shut the door,’” Mackinnon says, paraphrasing the Hollywood star. “I kind of wanted that spirit to be in this, because that’s what Edinburgh’s like during the festival. I wanted to put a paramedic drama at 3 o’clock in the morning in that environment.”As Rome’s MIA Market kicks off, Mackinnon says that “what’s exciting going into MIA is we’re at the beginning,” adding that he’s “looking for partners to build the series with me on an international level.”“MIA is amazing for seeing people’s eyes light up at a project and going, ‘Oh, we could do something with this.’ Because I do think that ‘BurnTime’ can travel as well as…[be] a returning brand,” he says. “It can exist in other festivals in other parts of the world. It could go to Brazil or Germany or South Africa and have its own version. I think it’s going to work anywhere.”With more than three decades of industry experience behind him, Mackinnon recently launched Rugged Island Films, a company that looks to capitalize on both his extensive body of work and Scotland’s production boom.“The idea is to use my experience with huge shows like ‘Sherlock’ and ‘Good Omens’ and ‘Outlander and ‘Line of Duty’ and ‘Doctor Who’ and build shows of that scale from Scotland,” he says. “Instead of having them come to us, we’re going to be looking outwards. I know how to make these shows, and I want to make some of my own now.”The company, which received slate funding from Screen Scotland, currently has roughly 10 series and five feature films in development, with MacKinnon bullish about expanding the outfit in the coming years.Most of all, he’s bullish on his native Scotland. “We’ve had a really fantastic run of series with ‘Dept. Q’ and ‘Good Omens’ and ‘Outlander.’ For a small country, that’s punching above our weight, and that’s where all of us in the industry want to keep it going,” he says. “We want to keep punching above our weight, not just making shows for ourselves; we want to make shows for the world. And we’ve got the skill set to do it.”There’s also the political will to make it happen, he says, pointing to programs like Lights, Camera, Capital, a new initiative launched by Screen Scotland and a consortium of Scottish business angels to bring together Scotland’s film and TV producing community with angel investors.“There’s so much going on. It’s very exciting,” he says. “I think in the U.K., outside London, we’re the most exciting spot to be.”

	The 12th edition of Rome’s MIA Market takes place Oct. 19 – 23.

schema.headline: ‘Line of Duty’ Director Douglas Mackinnon Preps Edinburgh-Set Paramedic Drama ‘BurnTime,’ Builds Slate at Rugged Island Films (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Comedy ‘Raging Moms,’ About Four Women Breaking Free in Midlife, Picked Up by Picture Tree (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Berlin-based Picture Tree International has boarded international sales on “Raging Moms” (Komplizinnen), an ensemble comedy from the production com
body:
Berlin-based Picture Tree International has boarded international sales on “Raging Moms” (Komplizinnen), an ensemble comedy from the production company behind successes like “Weekend Rebels,” “Welcome to Germany,” “Never Look Away” and “The Lives of Others.”

	PTI will screen the film as a market premiere for buyers at the upcoming American Film Market, with Leonine Studios releasing the film in German theaters on Jan. 21.
	

	Menopause, empty nests and romantic misadventures upend the lives of four women, who have had enough of being reasonable. As they abandon familiar roles and make increasingly reckless choices, their paths collide in a comedy about friendship and the messy business of starting over.


	The cast is led by Laura Tonke (“Amrum,” “The People vs. Fritz Bauer”), Heike Makatsch (“The Book Thief,” “Love Actually”), Katharina Marie Schubert (“The Teachers’ Lounge”) and Anne Ratte-Polle (“Dark,” “Undine”), with Tom Schilling (“Never Look Away,” “Generation War”), Christoph Maria Herbst (“Contra,” “How About Adolf”) and Trystan Pütter (“Babylon Berlin,” “Toni Erdmann”) also starring.

	“Raging Moms” is written and directed by Sonja Heiss, whose credits include “When Will It Be Again Like It Never Was Before,” which earned her a German Film Award nomination for Best Director.

	A Wiedemann & Berg Film production, “Raging Moms” is produced by Johanna Bergel, Quirin Berg and Max Wiedemann, with funding from the German Federal Film Fund (DFFF), the German Federal Film Board (FFA), Medienboard Berlin-Brandenburg and FFF Bayern.
	

	PTI’s AFM lineup also includes market screenings of a newly remastered 4K version of “The Experiment,” from “Downfall” director Oliver Hirschbiegel, and Constantin Film’s “The Perfect Holiday,” Bora Dagtekin’s sequel to “The Perfect Secret,” the German remake of “Perfect Strangers.” Selected buyers will also be offered previews of the Uruguayan period thriller “Matarifes – Hunger for Change,” directed by Rafael and Bernardo Antonaccio (“In the Quarry”), and the Swedish tech satire “Push the Button,” directed by Anton Källrot and featuring Noah Taylor.

	Also upcoming on PTI’s slate include the historical biopic “Rafaela,” starring Loreto Mauleón, and “The Stolen Child,” the English-language, medieval fantasy epic written and directed by Sebastian McKinnon.

title: AI Could ‘Absolutely’ Replace Human Actors, CEO of Generative AI Startup Runway Says at Italy’s View Conference: ‘It’s Already Happening in a Way’
description: Durng a fireside chat entitled “Every Pixel Will Be Generated” at Turin’s View Conference,  an audience member asked Cristóbal Valenzuela, the co-C
body:
Durng a fireside chat entitled “Every Pixel Will Be Generated” at Turin’s View Conference,  an audience member asked Cristóbal Valenzuela, the co-CEO of generative AI startup Runway, whether AI could eventually replace human actors.

	“Yeah, absolutely. I think it’s already happening in a way,” he replied, going on to describe AI as “a new medium of expression” and “a new medium of storytelling.”


	His fellow speaker, Nvidia‘s Richard Kerris, was somewhat more attached to existing arrangements. Earlier in the session, he had recalled a director’s argument that the spontaneity between a director and an actor, such as Marlon Brando improvising with a cat on the set of “The Godfather,” could never be prompted. 
	

	“That craft is something to behold, and I just think that that’s something that I don’t think we’ll ever lose,” said Kerris, Nvidia VP of developer relations and general manager of media and entertainment. 

	“Not now, but I think models are going to get probably to a point where you can probably direct them in a very similar way,” Valenzuela replied.

	Kerris had also stressed that filmmaking still requires an understanding of character, composition and story. There is no “make movie button.”

	“I wish,” joked Valenzuela.

	A clear sense of what this might mean sits in Vaenzuela’s essay titled “It’s All About the Pixel Economy,” in which Valenzuela predicts that “the value of creating pixels is trending towards zero.” Eventually, he writes, the number of “seconds consumed” will converge with the number of “seconds generated.”
	

	Presently, a film often takes hundreds of people to make and millions of people two hours to watch. Valenzuela imagines a future where audiences generate personalized entertainment as quickly as they consume it.

	In another essay, “The Cost of a Frame,” Valenzuela charts a history of media through the cost of producing a credible frame. The relevant layer is the high production value content. It’s that tier in which Hollywood, and much of the conference’s professionals, work in.

	“This is the last expensive layer,” he writes and AI, he makes the case, is collapsing the cost of producing it.

	At the View fireside chat, Kerris frequently framed the resistance toward the technology as no different than the fears that previous tech advances stirred, including the emergence of computer-generated imagery. “The similarities of fear and rush to judgment on things is so similar to what I’ve seen in the past,” he said.

	Jeff Kember, Nvidia’s principal technical evangelist for media, painted a similarly optimistic vision in his presentation, “Creative Control in the Age of AI Agents,” claiming that adoption is already widespread.

	“There’s a whole bunch of people talking about how they’re using generative AI and then there’s also a bunch of people who aren’t talking about it and they’re not talking about it primarily because their legal team is not letting them talk about it,” he said. ‘But both people on each side of this fence are both using generative AI. I don’t know anyone who isn’t.”

	Between sessions a number of VFX artists, game studio heads, and animation directors spoke less of fear and more of anger relating to something peculiar and unique to the generative models, namely the material used to train on in the first place.

	Asked by Variety about the training data behind the models, Valenzuela said one of the “core misbeliefs” about AI was that “people thought AI was some sort of a database.”

	“They’re not databases,” he said. “They’re learning from representation.”

	It seems an unavoidable concern with the courts, the likely arbiter. In July, a federal judge approved Anthropic’s settlement of $1.5 billion with authors whose books were downloaded from pirate libraries. A prior ruling had found that using copyrighted works to train models could constitute fair use, while distinguishing that question from the company’s acquisition and retention of pirated copies. Meanwhile, there are a number of lawsuits against many of the biggest AI companies still going through the legal system. One is a proposed class action case by visual artists against Stability AI, Midjourney, DeviantArt and Runway itself. It alleges that their copyrighted work was used to develop the generative models without compensation or permission.
	

	Taken together the talks from the companies leading the charge in AI at View Conference revealed a worldview whereby the cost of generating moving images approaches zero and at the least the traditional structures of production are fundamentally reshaped.

title: ‘Big Boys Don’t Cry’ Director Muhammad Mustapha Talks Masculinity Ahead of El Gouna Premiere: ‘The Only Emotion Men Are Allowed to Express Is Anger’
description: Egyptian filmmaker Muhammad Mustapha’s “Big Boys Don’t Cry” follows a group of Cairo bodybuilders and nightclub bouncers, offering a view into how
body:
Egyptian filmmaker Muhammad Mustapha’s “Big Boys Don’t Cry” follows a group of Cairo bodybuilders and nightclub bouncers, offering a view into how men understand and perform masculinity.

	The documentary, which had its world premiere in the Feature Documentary Competition at Egypt’s El Gouna Film Festival, grew out of Mustapha’s curiosity about this particular group of men and questions about his own understanding of masculinity.
	

	“I’m a feminist. I’m intellectual. I find myself very drawn to this hyper-masculine performance,” he tells Variety. “I should know better, right? And so this was the question: Why am I so intrigued?”


	Mustapha distinguishes that curiosity from a desire to investigate something he saw as inherently wrong. When he began the project in 2016, he approached it as an anthropological and sociological study of masculinity and how it is expressed in different contexts.

	His own upbringing gave him a point of reference. Mustapha grew up in what he describes as a “local” Cairo neighborhood, where he was surrounded by its masculine codes. As a studious “nerd,” he could be seen as less masculine there. But when he entered dental school, the same behavior could instead make him appear loud or vulgar.

	That contrast helped him recognize how masculinity could shift according to context, a fact he also saw among the men he was observing.

	“How they perform their masculinity on stage is different than in front of the pub, is different than when he is addressing a problem, different than when he is with his family,” he says.
	

	It took roughly three years for that initial exploration to develop into a film, as Mustapha’s relationship with the men deepened and he was forced to examine his own views of masculinity.

	That relationship also informed how “Big Boys Don’t Cry” was made. Mustapha rejects the idea that documentary filmmaking can ever be entirely observational, arguing that a camera inevitably changes what happens in front of it. The men became collaborators, at times proposing situations themselves.

	“I wouldn’t say I made this film alone. I would say I made it with the characters. We made it together.”

	One of the film’s central figures is Abdallah, with whom Mustapha spent a year before filming began. Mustapha initially believed the film would be driven by its ideas about masculinity, only to discover in the edit that their friendship had become its emotional throughline.



	

					Muhammad Mustapha
									Courtesy of Hassala Films
	



	“I thought there was no emotional arc in the film. It was very theme-driven, and it was very intellectual,” he recalls. “At the end, while we were editing, I discovered that the emotional core of the film is actually our friendship.”

	Building that relationship also meant giving the men control over what they shared. Participants could ask for material to be removed throughout the process, including during the final edit.

	“I earned their trust. It was not given to me,” he affirms.

	The absence of women is equally intentional. Mustapha wanted to observe the men in an exclusively male environment, which he compares to peeking into a gym locker room. Introducing women, he believed, would “change the equation.”

	For Mustapha, the questions at the heart of “Big Boys Don’t Cry” extend far beyond Egypt. While masculinity takes different forms across cultures, he sees restrictions on men’s emotional expression as painfully universal.

	“The only emotion men are allowed to express is anger,” he argues. “Imagine how distorted the male psyche is because of all this suppression of emotions.”

	The El Gouna premiere brings “Big Boys Don’t Cry” back to a major stop in its development. Mustapha brought the project to CineGouna, the festival’s industry arm, in 2020 before it went on to receive support from the Doha Film Institute, Red Sea Film Fund and Germany’s Robert Bosch Foundation.
	

	“It’s a full circle moment,” he reflects. “I’m very excited to show it to people in Egypt, though I’m slightly nervous.”

	The film’s decade-long development has also led Mustapha to reflect on how independent films are made in Egypt and the region. He wants filmmakers to take more artistic risks and focus on local audiences rather than on the whims of international festivals and programmers.

	“We need to work with less budget, with less financial risk, and more artistic risks.”

	And above all: “Tell our stories to our audience.”

schema.headline: ‘Big Boys Don’t Cry’ Director Muhammad Mustapha Talks Masculinity Ahead of El Gouna Premiere: ‘The Only Emotion Men Are Allowed to Express Is Anger’

title: Merged Banijay, All3Media Entity Sets Top Brass Comprised of Banijay Execs
description:
The newly-merged Banijay/All3Media entity, officially now known as Banijay Entertainment, has unveiled its senior leadership team.

	Joining CEO Ma
body:
The newly-merged Banijay/All3Media entity, officially now known as Banijay Entertainment, has unveiled its senior leadership team.

	Joining CEO Marco Bassetti, deputy CEO Jane Turton and Banijay Rights CEO Cathy Payne on the executive team will be Fred Balmary as chief business officer, Nicolas Chazarain as chief legal officer, Thomas Gousset as chief finance officer and Anne Van Sprang as chief human resources officer.


	Bassetti also confirmed that Lucas Green will stay on as chief content officer for operations, James Townley as chief content officer for development and Kate Humphreys as chief communications officer.
	

	They will all report to Bassetti.

	Other than Turton, who was previously CEO of All3Media, all of the team originate from Banijay, with most of them also pre-dating Banijay’s 2020 acquisition of Endemol Shine, including Balmary, Chazarain, Van Sprang, Humphreys and Green. Gousset joined Banijay just a few months before the Endemol deal completed. Of the group, Townley is the only one who came from Endemol itself.

	In a company-wide memo, Bassetti wrote: “Since their appointments, this group has made a significant contribution to the business, with many playing an integral role in delivering the merger and advancing the current integration – please join me in congratulating them as we embark on this next chapter.”

	He added: “We will formally introduce the team across the business as the integration progresses. In the meantime, we appreciate your patience as we continue through this period of change.”

	All3Media’s Thomas Shearer and Jamie McIntyre-Brown are also staying on as deputy CFO and deputy CLO respectively.
	

	Banijay’s merger with All3Media – which has also seen it sunset the All3Media brand – completed in July. The new behemoth, which is chaired by Redbird IMI’s Jeff Zucker, now owns dozens of production companies across the world as well as superbrands raging from “The Traitors” to “Peaky Blinders.”

title: Atlanta Technical College Student Accidentally Shoots Classmate, Kills Himself
description:

                          Man Accidentally Shoots Classmate
body:
Atlanta Technical College Shooting
                          Man Accidentally Shoots Classmate
                          ... Kills Himself
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            A student is dead and another is injured after an accidental shooting at Atlanta Technical College Monday.
      
    
            Atlanta police say one student was carrying a gun that had accidentally discharged inside a classroom, hitting another student in the leg and injuring them.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Investigators say the student with the gun then left the classroom and reportedly went to the bathroom, where he died of an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound.
      

            The police department's report says an ambulance brought the injured student to the hospital.
      
    
            The report says the injured student was alert, conscious and breathing when officers responded at 8:45 AM, and the college said they are expected to recover.
      
    
            Police say this was an isolated incident and believe there's no active threat to the community. The college says the campus was secured afterward and operations have since resumed.

title: Sam Altman Rips His Sister, Claims She's Thirsty for Attention In Court Battle
description:
Sam Altman On Sister
                          My Sister's Thirsty For Attention ...
body:
Sam Altman On Sister
                          My Sister's Thirsty For Attention ...
                          She Leaked Video From Court Battle
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Sam Altman is calling out his sister, who is suing him for alleged abuse, claiming she is using her lawsuit to gain more social media followers ... TMZ has learned. 
      
    
            We obtained court docs filed by the tech billionaire ... and he's slamming Ann Altman for posting portions of her recent deposition on X, TikTok, and other platforms. 
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Sam wants the court to order Ann to confirm she has destroyed all confidential videos and transcripts of her deposition within 3 days.
      

            In his motion, Sam says Ann and her lawyers have repeatedly "and incorrectly" insisted that she should have the right to publish the entirety of her depo video online ... which Sam says should not be released. 
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Sam even claims her lawsuit is really just a ploy to gain internet clout ... he says, "There is serious reasons to believe that [Ann's] true purpose in bringing this lawsuit was not to litigate her claims in good faith but rather to create discovery that she can use to drive traffic to her social media accounts and podcasts."
      
    
            He is asking the court to intervene immediately. 
      
    
            As TMZ previously reported, Ann sued Sam for alleged childhood sexual abuse when she was 3 and he was 12. Sam adamantly denied the claims. The lawsuit is seeking unspecified damages for alleged PTSD. Sam countersued Ann for $1 and had several family members back him up in court.
